Prologue.

It is certainly not the least noble jewel: of the treasury, of evangelical preaching, the foundation of natural things: for the purpose of providing examples and comparisons. As the redemptive use of such examples and comparisons: the more familiar they are to listeners, both in words and in the most commonly used language and expression, the more useful and beneficial they will be. For this purpose this work was made, a true treasure: at great cost and labor: written here in the Mexican language: the properties and outward characteristics, as far as could be attained: of animals, birds, and fish: trees, herbs, and flowers, the most well known and used, that exist throughout this land: where there is a great wealth of vocabulary in this language: very proper and very common: and very pleasing subject matter. It will also be useful for making understood the value of creatures: so that they are not belittled: because any creature that is seen as eminent, whether in good or in bad, is called teotl, which means god: thus the sun was called teotl: for its splendor: and others for their greatness and ferocity: and many animals were also called thus for their terrible disposition and bravery. From which it follows that this name is taken in both a good and a bad sense. And this is much better understood when the full word is used: teopiltontli, a very beautiful child: teopiltontli, a very wicked boy. Many other words are composed in this same manner: from whose meaning one can conjecture that this word teotl, means: something extreme, whether in good or in bad. Thus the present volume may be held or esteemed as a treasure, of the language and vocabulary of the Mexican tongue: and a very rich treasury of the things that exist in this land.

To the sincere reader.

You have, dear reader, in the present volume: a forest with a great diversity of mountains and crags: where you will find wild trees of every kind: fierce beasts and serpents. You have a garden populated with all manner of fruit-bearing trees, and of many kinds: where there are strong and cold streams of many sorts. It is full of birds, animals, and fish of every kind. You have a very delightful grove, full of all manner of flowers: both those that grow on trees, shrubs, and bushes: and those that grow in the fields: in it there are birds with sweet and rich plumage: and also gardens, built to a thousand wonders: you have a diversity of children and buildings: you have likewise fields and plains, where there are all manner of plants and herbs: where there are pools and lagoons: where reeds, cattails, and rushes grow: and a diversity of small aquatic and terrestrial animals. Where there are mines, of all manner of precious stones: and of many other things useful to life. Where there are our kinds of soils, stones, waters, and hills. The order set out above is not followed, but rather the following. The first chapter deals with the animals of the water: such as fish and other animals. p. 2. It contains seven paragraphs. The second deals with birds: it contains ten paragraphs. b. 20. The third chapter deals with the animals of the water: such as fish and other animals that live in the water: it contains five paragraphs. The fourth deals with fierce animals: b. 61. in the water: it contains four paragraphs. b. 70. The fifth deals with serpents and others. b. 77.

Book Eleventh

Book Eleventh on the properties of animals, birds, fish, trees, herbs, flowers, metals, and stones, and of colors.

Chapter One, on animals.

First paragraph on wild beasts.

The tiger walks and lives in the mountains, among the crags and cliffs, and also in the water. It is noble, and they say it is a prince and lord of the other animals. It is shrewd and cautious and pampers itself like a cat, and endures no labor whatsoever. It is disgusted to see filthy things and avoids them, and holds itself in high regard. It is low-bodied and stout, and has a long tail, and its forepaws are thick and wide, and it has a thick neck,

This eleventh book speaks of the various living creatures: of birds, of fish, of trees, of herbs, of things lying in the earth made of metal, of stone, of other things, and of various stones.

This first chapter speaks of living creatures and how they move about.

This first paragraph speaks of beasts of prey.

The ocelot: dweller of the forests, dweller of the rocky places, dweller of the water; a noble, a commoner. They say it surpasses all other animals in cunning. It is knowing, self-aware, ever attentive, never a scavenger, never an eater of filth, never a devourer of corruption. Noble, yet base. It is long, lean, cylindrical in body, broad and flat-headed, thick-bodied, thick-fleshed, thick with muscle, with a long tail, with a rounded tail, with large palms, with flat palms, with a thick neck, with a broad neck, with a round head, with a large round head...

Concerning Animals, folio 2.

It has a large head; the ears are small; the snout is thick, fleshy, and short, and dark in color; its haunches are fatty; it has a broad face; its eyes are bright like burning coals; its fangs are large and thick; its teeth are small, little, and sharp; the molars wide at the top; and the mouth very wide; and it has long, sharp claws; it has thick necks on the forelegs and on the hind legs; and it has a white chest; it has a bright chest, and as it grows it becomes spotted, and its claws grow, and likewise its teeth grow, and its molars and fangs; and it snarls and bites and tears with its teeth and cuts; it growls, and roars making a sound like a trumpet.

The white tiger: they say it is the captain of the other tigers and is very white. There are others that are whitish, spotted with black.

There is another tiger of [long] hair

[Right column — Nahuatl text describing physical and behavioral attributes of the ocelot, its sounds, movements, and color variants:]

It is rough-eared, thick-lipped, thick-nosed, stout-snouted, hard-snouted, with folded jowls, with folds on its cheeks; flat-faced, with a rough face; with a smooth jaw, marked with black, spotted, speckled; ocelot-colored, curled, rolling about in curled fashion, curling itself, rolling about like an ocelot; it crouches, it compresses itself, it springs up, it rises up coiling like a serpent, it bounds, it leaps about, it tears apart, it crackles, it cries out, it screams, it sounds like a trumpet.

The white ocelot: they say it is the leader of the ocelots; it is white and very white. Some say we cannot catch it; it is spotted, it is marked with black, it leaps upward.

The red ocelot: it is very red, very tawny, all spotted,

Book Eleven

...red and spotted with black.

¶The nature of the tiger [jaguar] is that it eats animals, such as deer and rabbits and other similar creatures. It is fastidious and not suited for labor; it takes great care to keep itself clean; and at night it can see the animals it is going to hunt — it has very keen sight, and even if it is very dark, or even if there is fog, it can see very small things.
When it sees the hunter with his bow and arrows, it does not flee, but rather sits looking at him, without hiding behind anything or pressing up against anything. Then it begins to hiss, and that breath it directs toward the hunter, in order to instill fear and dread in him and make his heart faint with the hissing. And the hunter then begins to shoot at it; and the first arrow, which is made of cane, the jaguar catches with its paw and breaks it to pieces with its teeth, and begins to snarl and growl, and as another arrow is shot at it...

[Nahuatl column:]
¶This is how it lives: the ocelot goes about seeking, pursuing, those it will eat — deer, rabbits, etc. And it is very fastidious: it is not crude; it is very refined, it grooms itself, it washes itself, it cleans its face, it licks itself; it is deceptive, boastful; it is very alert, it is very prepared. And with its sight it looks at, it observes, what it seeks to eat, what it hunts; it sees very well, its gaze is sharp and clear, seeing well at a distance: even in darkness, even in dimness, it sees. When it sees, when it encounters, when it faces its adversary — it does not lower its head, it does not look down; it stands facing it squarely. It settles itself well, it crouches for nothing — the jaguar. Then it begins to snort, to blow its breath, so as to terrify the hunter, to make his heart stop, the one shooting at it. And then the hunter begins to shoot at it; one arrow that he launches — of cane — the jaguar simply catches it and pulls it and snaps it apart, and slaps at it...

Concerning animals                    fo. 3

He does the same. The hunters kept the custom that they were not to shoot the jaguar more than four arrows: this was their tradition or devotion. And if they did not kill it with those four arrows, the hunter would consider himself defeated. And the jaguar then begins to stretch itself, and to shake itself, and to lick itself. Having done this, it gathers itself and leaps as if flying, and throws itself upon the hunter. Even if the hunter is ten or twenty fathoms away, it takes but one leap; it goes all bristled up, like a cat against a dog. Then it kills the hunter and eats him. Skilled hunters, upon shooting the first arrow — if the jaguar was not shattered by it — take a leaf from an oak tree, and from another similar tree, and fix it onto the arrow, and shoot the jaguar with it. The leaf placed thus makes a sound, just as when a grasshopper flies and falls to the ground halfway, or nearby.

[Nahuatl column:] Making noises with its throat, snarling, it becomes enraged, as it is said. It throws itself at him just as many times as it shoots arrows at him, doing so in the same manner. And if the count of arrows shot at it falls short, even by one, the arrow flies: then it looks at the hunter. At dawn it yawns, stretches, shakes, quivers, cleans itself, flutters its sides. Then it truly readies itself; it stretches out its claws and flies off — ten measures away, the arrow stands erect in the air; even to the far side, twenty measures: it goes seizing it, for once it leaps: it flies, curves, circles around, surrounds — there the arrow dies; there it is consumed. And when it recovers: the hunter shoots another arrow, takes a reed, pulls it toward himself the quauhxiuatlapalli [eagle-herb board], and places the reed-tip there, and the reed comes out singing. He shoots it again, and it rustles as it goes: the acazoatl reed. Just as a grasshopper goes: perhaps it strikes the ground, perhaps it lands beside it, flying, falling, into the quauhxiuatlapalli: it cures its eyes with it.

Book Eleven

of the tiger: with this the tiger diverts itself from striking the leaf that falls, and the arrow reaches and passes through it or wounds it; and then the tiger leaps upward and coming back down to the ground, sits again as it was before. And there it dies seated, without closing its eyes; although it is dead, it appears alive. When the tiger hunts, it first breathes upon whatever it is going to catch with that breath, stunning it. The flesh of the tiger has a bad taste and burns.

¶ There was a people who were like assassins, who were called nonohzalequc; they were practiced and bold people, ready to kill. They carried with them the skin of the tiger — a piece of the forehead, another piece of the chest, and at the end of the tail the claws, and the heart, and the fangs, and the snouts. They said that with these things they were strong, and bold, and terrifying when bound together; and everyone feared them, and they feared no one, because of carrying these things of the tiger. These are also called pixeque teiolpachwanj.

¶ The wildcat [lynx], they call it by this name, which is to say tlaco ocelutl, tlacomjztli, because

[Nahuatl column:]
It shoots them, it strikes them from afar; it is very swift; and then the ocelot crouches down. And then it settles itself flat on the ground, stretches itself out, presses itself low; it thus positions itself as it was before, its eyes rolling; it dies thus; only with its eyes open. Though it appears yet alive. When the ocelot feeds: first it makes the prey afraid of it, it causes it to be stunned, it causes it to be confused. Its flesh is very hot and bitter.

¶ The nonohzalequc: it is said they go about with the skin of the ocelot's face, and the skin of its chest, and the tip of its tail, and its blood, and its heart, and its rattle — that is, its spine — and its muzzle; they say that thus they go about invulnerable, that thus they go about making others afraid of them, that thus they are feared: that no one dares face them, for they go about under their protection; they go by the name nonohzalequc, pixeque, teiolpathoanj.

¶ The tlaco ocelutl [wildcat]: what is said of it — tlacomjztli: it is small, it is short-tailed, it is a young one; in Castilian it is called [cat]. And nexcoac...

Of Animals                                                    folio 4.

which is small, the size of a cat: it is brown, has some dark spots like a tiger or painted animal.

There is an animal in this land called tlacaxolotl: it is large, bigger than a great ox, it has a large head, a long snout, very wide ears, it has large teeth and molars: but in the form of a person, it has a very thick and sturdy neck, it has thick feet and hands, hooves like an ox but larger: it has large and wide haunches, its tail is thick and long: it is the color of a red ox, it has very thick hide: its meat is edible: they say its meat and flavor contains that of all animals, roots, and even of men. This animal is rare, it lives in the provinces of Atzaccan, and of Tepuztontlan, and Tlanguylapan, which are toward Honduras, it lives in the mountains and in certain places among the cliffs: it eats wild peanuts.

Tlacaxolotl, it greatly surpasses the cow: its head is very large and long-necked: its flesh is very thick and meaty: its teeth are very large: it appears roughly person-like, its neck is very thick and very fleshy: its shin, its leg, its body is very hairy and rough, very large, its mane is rough and shaggy, not smooth: its snout very large, its tail very thick, very long, not easily cut: its hair all over is not very long, like a deer's hair: its hide is dark-colored. This tlacaxolotl eats many things: and the flavor of its flesh is not in one part only — it has the taste of all kinds of meat: of human meat, of wild beast meat, of deer, of turkey, of dog. This tlacaxolotl, it lives only midway between — it dwells in Atzaccan, Tepuztontlan, Tlangutylapan, there in the great forest where no one can reach the interior. When it feeds it [illegible] when...

Book Eleven

These are the cacahuates called quappatlachtli. It also eats green corn and corn cobs. When it comes upon a cornfield, it eats everything, leaving nothing behind. When food is scarce, it eats the leaves of shrubs and trees. When it defecates, it expels the cacao beans whole, nearly a jarful of them each time. The inhabitants of that land go searching for its dung in order to collect the cacao it has passed. This animal does not fear people, nor does it die from an arrow. They catch it by digging a large pit and covering it with branches and grass so that it falls in; there they kill it, and from there they pull it out with ropes and eat its flesh, which is very good to eat.

And it cries out among the trees in the forest. When it finds nothing to eat, this animal called Jeucacaoatl, also quappatlahtli, goes to the cornfields and takes corn one ear at a time. It scatters the cacao, and it is good at carrying loads on its back. The commoners go looking for it in the forest so that they can collect the cacao from it. It is not timid, nor does it die from arrows, even if it is wounded. It does not dig burrows; it goes all about searching among the stones and rocks, and it goes far into the woods. When they have found it, they lay logs and stones over it and cover it.

Concerning animals. Folio 5.

[Spanish, left column:]
There is an animal called tzonistac. It is found toward the South Sea, in the province of Toztlan and Casepan. It is called tzonistac because it has a very white head only. It is about the size of a tiger, more or less. It is low to the ground and thick-bodied. It eats the flesh of wild beasts. When it wishes to hunt, it snarls like a cat and then suddenly seizes its prey. It has hands and feet like a tiger. Its entire body is very black, and it has a long tail. This animal

[Nahuatl, upper right:]
there: and then it goes and twists itself upon the person there, it tears him apart, and thus he dies there; then afterwards it drags him away with its mouth.

[Nahuatl, lower right:]
Tzonistac: it is a beast of prey. It lives over there in Tozllantzapan, somewhat near the great sea. The reason it is called tzonistac is that its head is very white, and it is white down to the neck; it is quite large in body, about the size of an ocelot — somewhat thick, somewhat flat. It goes about stalking the animals that roam about. When it sees them, it immediately growls loudly, it gnashes its teeth; then it leaps upon them; then, just like an ocelot, it is very agile, flying through the air upon them.

Book Eleven

It appears very rarely; and if someone encounters it and sees that its head is yellow, it is a sign that he will die soon. And if someone encounters it and its head appears white, it is a sign that he will live long in poverty even though he works very hard. This omen was associated with this animal: they kill it with an arrow.

[Nahuatl column:]
Its entire body is shining and glistening; its tail is long, just as that of the ocelot. And if one sees it with a white head, no one can look upon whoever encounters it; if one who sees it does not become ill from the encounter — then that person will live a very long time, will endure long, though he suffers greatly; and even more so it is said: if such and such conditions are met, and in such a way it is received, whoever eats of the animal's broth thereby gains something, for it reaches and overtakes them.

Of Animals. Folio 6.

[partial Nahuatl text at top, partially illegible]

This animal, by its description, appears to be a bear; and if it is not a bear, I do not know what animal among those we know it can be compared to. It is a hairy animal, with long wool: it has a tail, very woolly, like that of a fox; but of a dark brownish color, it has shaggy wool; when it is old: it has small, narrow ears; it has a round face, wide, almost like that of a person; it has a thick snout; it has a little gland for being venomous, to poison whatever it encounters; the vapor or air that it emits is of many colors, like a rainbow; it is very cunning, and lies in ambush to kill.

The lion: it is the size of a tiger, it is not spotted; it also has sleek fur; and in body it is like a tiger, except that it has larger claws, and also small ones very long; it is rarely dark; there are red lions and others whitish: these are called white lions.

Cujtlachtli [the bear/wolverine]: or also called cueclachtli; it is thick, rounded, very large, with a broad tail base, [its tail hairs spread out]; its [fur] is very rounded and smooth; it cannot [easily] be compared to our [animals]; it is somewhat like a chichimec person in appearance, very large and broad; it is very round-faced, very clear-eyed, it sees those who approach it; it is just like a rainbow coming from its mouth; it is very knowing, it can imitate people and make itself known; it rolls upon people, it makes itself known, it causes flatulence.

Miztli [the mountain lion/puma]: it is just like the ocelot in size and appearance: there is nothing that can be placed alongside it; it is entirely slender, narrow, exactly alike, very long and lean, very lean and straight; it leaps very well, it is dark-smoked in color; the reddish puma is tawny-colored; the [other kind of] puma — in some [accounts] it is called the white puma.

Book Eleven

¶This animal, which is called the quaumiztli [tree-lion/ocelot], by its properties appears to be an onza [lynx/wildcat]. And if it is not one, no other animal seems so similar: they say it resembles a lion, except that it always lives in the trees, leaping from branch to branch, and there it seeks its food. It rarely comes down to the ground.

¶There is an animal in these parts called the maçamiztli [deer-lion]. The name means a certain kind of lion. It is not known whether it exists anywhere else. It is the size of a deer, and has the color of a deer, and has claws like a deer's, and the males have horns like a deer; but it has feet like a lion, very sharp, and teeth and fangs like a lion. It does not eat plants. It lives among the other deer. And when it wants to eat, it embraces a deer and grips it by the neck; it opens it through the belly, eating from the legs up to the throat, and in this way draws out all the intestines and eats them. In nothing do the other deer associate with it, except through a foul stench that it carries.

¶The quaumiztli [tree-lion]: it lives only as the mountain lion lives, always dwelling in the treetops and in the high crags. If it eats anything, it rarely comes down to the ground.

¶The maçamiztli [deer-lion]: it is called by this name because it resembles a deer in certain ways, yet is truly like a mountain lion. The females resemble doe-deer in appearance; it has a long tail. It approaches and comes near; it is truly like a mountain lion in its nature, and none can escape it, none can flee from it once it has seized a deer. Thereupon the deer-lion tears it: it tears it open and devours it. It is extremely large and very fat. It seizes prey in its claws like iron hooks. Whatever it takes, whatever it catches, it strips off the skin, peels it entirely. It is greatly to be feared; it wanders seeking to devour, it never rests in peace.

Of animals.                         160.
                                    folio 7.
in the middle, in the center. And in the morning, when day breaks, it throws itself down; it rolls in the dung; it is a wildcat. And yet it knows how to recognize itself. It goes about scattering things.

There is another animal in this land called the cujtlamjztli, which means "bastard lion." According to what is said of it, it is a wolf: it eats dogs and chickens and sheep. In wintertime it secludes itself until it can no more, and then it goes about hunting for three days without stopping. For this reason they call it "bastard lion," because it is a glutton; it has no den like the lions; and at night it eats the chickens and the sheep; and even so, this beast kills all the chickens and sheep it can.

The cujtlamjztli lives in the forest, it wanders through the ravines, like the mountain lion. It goes about at night, the cujtlamjztli. It seizes animals; it hunts and captures them; it takes four, or it seizes them in its jaws. Two days, three days it goes without eating, then all at once it gorges itself; it comes down from above, and thus it is called cujtlamjztli, because it is voracious and also because it does not shelter itself. At night it then comes to eat the turkey; it is like the large wild beast. It also looks like a wildcat and also like a dog.

There is another animal called iteujn quanjs, which means "camel of dogs," which is of the same kind as the one described above. They are called by this name iteujn quanjs, or camels of dogs, because at night—

It approaches the settlements and from nearby begins to howl; and all the dogs that hear it respond by howling, and go running to where it is. Second paragraph on animals such as foxes, wolves, and other similar animals.

There is in this land an animal called coyote, which some Spaniards call a fox and others call a wolf; but according to its characteristics, it is neither wolf nor fox, but an animal proper to this land. It is very shaggy with long fur, has a thick and very woolly tail; it has small, pointed ears; its snout is long and not very thick, and dark; its legs are sinewy; its claws are curved and black. It is very alert and cautious. To hunt, it crouches down and lies in wait, looking in all directions to catch its prey. It is very cunning in ambushing its game. When it wants to rush at the prey, it first hurls itself—

Coyote: it has a long, blunt snout; it is wide-faced; it has long legs, long-legged, slender-legged; it is pinched at the temples, sleek-headed, dark-throated, white-eared, white-toed; its paws are dark, it shows well, it knows things. How it hunts: it stalks crouching, it presses itself low; it rolls in the grass, it stretches itself on the ground; it sets itself thus, it crouches. It watches keenly in all directions; it knows a person from afar. It launches itself forward. It seeks sheep(?); it seizes game...

This snake was one of those called cincoatl. And the traveler

This animal eats raw meat, and also dried and green ears of corn, and green stalks, and hens, and bread, and honey. Third paragraph concerning other small animals like squirrels and similar ones.

There are many kinds of squirrels in this land: some of them are somewhat large and elongated, and are brown in color; they have soft fur, small ears like acorn cups, a bushy tail, with coarse fur dark at the tips. They eat whatever is available — bread, meat, and fruit — whatever they can get; even when driven away, they are not frightened, and for that reason do not leave off; they steal imperceptibly and eat whatever is stored. And for this reason thieves are called Tezhalutl. The cry of this little animal is thin and lively.

There are other squirrels that are raised in the mountains and in the trees; these squirrels eat pine nuts, and the tender buds of trees, and the worms that breed in the trees; they strip the bark from the trees in order to extract the worms that are inside.

The tree-squirrel: this one lives like the tezhalutl, it eats up on top of trees; it always stays in the treetops. And it is called the tree-squirrel because it eats the tender young pine cones, and also the tree-worms; it strips off the bark searching for them.

There are some little birds in this land that are very tiny, looking more like horseflies than birds. And when it begins to thunder, before it rains, it then wakes up and revives and is resurrected. It is medicinal for syphilitic sores, and whoever eats it will never have sores, but it makes sterile those who eat it.

[Nahuatl text:] Hummingbird: vitili, dark-colored, slender-billed, with a projecting lip, with a protruding beak, with a curved beak. It is a tree-clinger: it clings to trees, it plasters itself against them, it covers them, it spreads over them: it lays only one egg. It sips flowers: its food is flower nectar, flower syrup. It is hollow inside, fluffy, ash-colored, able to hang. It smooths the ground, licks up nectar, clings to trees: it drips, covers, spreads out, it flutters; it glides, it hangs, it squeaks. In its interior: it makes a sound, quauh-sound at its tip: there it cries out in the trees, scrapes along, begins to peel away. And in the cold season: it stiffens, it constricts, it shuts down: and then once more it revives. And when: it gurgles when it rains, then it rises, then it stirs, then it awakens. As a medicine for skin disease: whoever uses it will never have skin disease, it eats away the skin many times: yet it is swift, it makes itself erect.

There is another water bird called the teniztli, which means obsidian-stone beak. This bird flies at night and does not appear during the day. It is the size of a dove. It has three bills, one above another, and two mouths and two tongues; it eats through both mouths, but has only one gullet. These little birds go about in flocks together in the field, and when they are scattered, they come together again by calling to one another. On the Parts of the Tree
Folio 117.

The parts that a tree has are the following: roots — thick, thin, and round or cylindrical. These roots go down beneath the earth and reach deep into the ground; by means of them the tree holds fast to the earth and has its foundation.

The stock of the tree is thick and round; it has rough bark. From this stock the roots extend in all directions. The stock, where the roots are born, is strong and sturdy, very firmly pressed against the earth. The roots are its bonds; this stock sustains the whole tree, holding it upright.

The trunk of the tree rises from the stock; it is thick at the bottom and thinner toward the top; it is stout, cylindrical, and round.

It is knotty; from it grow twisted branches and straight ones. It has bark; it has hollows; some branches are cut; it has forks; it has dense and strong branches; it has some [branches...]

This herb is medicinal, and its seed is used for gout: grinding it and placing it on the spot where the gout is.

Second paragraph on mushrooms.

Mushrooms grow in fields and in the mountains; they are good to eat, they are cooked before eating. If they are eaten raw or poorly cooked, they cause vomiting, cramps, and death. To remedy the harm that mushrooms cause, the yellow ointment called Axin is good. It is applied with a syringe.

There are some of these mushrooms called Bontecomananacatl; they are large and round.

There are others called Xelhuasnanacatl; they grow in many clusters on one stem, some tall and some short.

Third paragraph concerning edible herbs that are cooked.

One of the herbs that is eaten cooked is called vauhquilit, which is amaranth. It is very green, has slender and somewhat tall branches, and broad leaves. The plants of this herb are called Vauhtli, and the seed of this herb is also called Vauhtli. This herb is grown to eat; it has a slightly sour taste. The water in which it is cooked is squeezed out before eating, and with salt, tamales are made from this herb, which are called quiltamalli. Tortillas are also made from ground maize and the leaves of this herb, and these are called quillaxcalli. This is a very common herb, and like the spinach of Castile, people eat a great deal of it.

Another herb that is eaten cooked is called quiltonilli. It has somewhat broad leaves when it is small. This herb is edible; when it is fully grown it is called petlicatl or opitsicatl. It is boiled with saltwater and the liquid is pressed out.

It is especially good for those who have relapsed from some illness, drinking it mixed with a pod of chili pepper and with seeds of squash, all ground together and mixed, drinking it two or three times and then taking a bath — this is how it heals. With the scrapings of the stone called Xiuhtomolteti. It also helps, in the manner described above, against the ailment of the heart that causes one to fall and to vomit, and one should drink it once or twice.

This stone is found near Xalapan, Yztepec, and Tlatlauhquitepec. The natives of those regions say that when it begins to thunder and rain in the mountains or hills, these stones fall from the clouds; in the mountains they go under the ground while still small, and each year they keep growing until they become large — some round, others long like truffles, some bigger, some smaller. The natives of that land say: wherever they see a single reed growing alone, they know the stone is there, and they go and dig it out. Healthy people may also drink it as described above; it tempers the body's heat.

[Nahuatl column:] It warms. And it is thus that it draws up the body's sustenance; it strikes fire. And it also clears one's vision. It is said of Xiuhtomolteti that it makes one sneeze repeatedly. It does not make a person very wicked at heart; it cools the passion in one's heart: once, or perhaps twice one will sneeze. The gold called teucuitlatl forms and grows within it, in its interior: it is just like the salapaneca stone. When it thunders, out there in the forest, in the ravines — not on rocky ground, but only in the flat earth — the gold (teucuitlatl) enters and falls there, just a tiny bit dropping down; it grows there for many years, becoming large, it develops. And when it has grown, the chaneques (earth spirits) notice it and reveal it: a single reed stands over the teucuitlatl, visible above the ground. When one goes to pull it out, it is very heavy, as if it were a bone — like a large bone — and some are just round. And also you should not go there when you are in a state of impurity; if our heart is troubled or agitated, it will not form properly. It is found at Iztepec, Xalapa, and Tlatlauhquitepec.

There are people who know where precious stones are found, and it is that any precious stone, wherever it may be, emits from itself a vapor or exhalation like a fine smoke; and this smoke appears when the sun is about to rise, or at the rising of the sun. Those who search for and know these stones, place themselves in a convenient spot when the sun is about to rise, and look toward where the sun comes up, and where they see a fine little mist rising, they then know that there, there is a precious stone, or that one has formed there, or that one is hidden there. And they go to that place, and if they find some stone from which that little mist was rising, they understand that inside it there is some precious stone, and they break it open to look for it.

[Nahuatl column:]
It is seen upon it: wherever it goes, it rolls along, it travels about, or somewhere it drifts along, it goes skimming along. And so the mother of the precious stone does not carry it; it is placed somewhere — it may be small, or perhaps on its surface, not very large, just a little bit, just a small amount, just a little, just a tiny bit — in the place where it was set. And those who are knowledgeable, who take heed of these things, they among themselves perceive it: by this means they recognize it, they see it clearly — for it steams, it glimmers; at dawn, just before sunrise it comes out, and they seek it where it places itself, where it stands — they go to meet the sun; and when the sun comes out, with its full face it truly gazes upon it, it shines very brightly, it dazzles; it gleams very brightly: in that place where the smoke rises like a little puff of mist, they see it clearly, the shining serpent-like gleam; it is then taken — the precious stone — whether it be a green stone, or a clear crystal, or some other sparkling gem.

For the ancient inhabitants of this land believed that the sky meets the water in the sea, as if it were a house, where the water forms the walls and the sky is the ceiling above them.
